problem.paragraph: Take any $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$H$$ —say, $$\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$ —and take any $$c \neq 1$$ —say, $$c = 2$$ . Then $$c\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 6 \\ 14 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . If this is in $$H$$ , then there is some $$s$$ such that $$\begin{bmatrix} 3 s \\ 2 + 5 s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 14 \end{bmatrix}$$

The subset $$S$$ is a subspace of $$M_{3 \times 3}$$ since it satisfies all three of the requirements listed in the definition of a subspace:

list.item: Observe that the $$\textbf{0}$$ in $$M_{3 \times 3}$$ is the $$3 \times 3$$ zero matrix and since $$\textbf{0}^{T} = \textbf{0}$$ , the matrix $$0$$ is symmetric and hence $$0$$ is in $$S$$ .

Let $$A$$ and $$B$$ in $$S$$ . Notice that $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$3 \times 3$$ symmetric matrices so $$A^{T} = A$$ and $$B^{T} = B$$ . By the properties of transposes of matrices, $$(A + B)^{T} = A^{T} + B^{T} = A + B$$ . Thus $$A + B$$ is symmetric and hence $$A + B$$ is in $$S$$ .

Let $$A$$ be in $$S$$ and let $$c$$ be a scalar. Since $$A$$ is symmetric, by the properties of symmetric matrices, $$(cA)^{T} = c(A^{T}) = cA$$ . Thus $$cA$$ is also a symmetric matrix and hence $$cA$$ is in $$S$$ .
